subject: Critical Thinking
subcategory: Evidence & Truth: How We Know What's Real
title: Evaluating Sources in the Information Age
description: A micro-lesson that makes Evaluating Sources in the Information Age usable.

hook.text: A blog post, a peer-reviewed paper, & a TikTok video all claim the same thing. Are they equally trustworthy?

buildup.text: CRAAP test: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose. Five questions to evaluate any information source.

discovery.text: Who wrote it? What are their credentials? When was it published? What evidence supports it? Who funded it?

twist.text: Professional-looking websites can be completely false. Ugly forums can contain expert knowledge. Don't judge by design.

climax.text: The best habit: trace claims to their primary source. If a news article cites a study, read the study.

punchline.text: Don't trust the headline. Read the source behind it.

quiz.question: What does the CRAAP test evaluate?
options: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, and Purpose of sources
The quality of a website's design

details.summary: Evaluating sources requires checking credentials, methodology, potential bias, publication venue, and corroboration. In the information age, anyone can publish, making source evaluation more critical and more difficult than ever.
details.whyItMatters: The explosion of online information means you encounter more claims daily than any previous generation. Source evaluation is your primary defense against misinformation.
takeaways: Check the author's credentials and potential conflicts of interest
Evaluate the methodology behind any empirical claim
Seek corroboration from independent, reputable sources

faq.question: What is the quickest way to evaluate an online source's credibility?
faq.answer: Use lateral reading: open new tabs and search for what others say about the source before diving into its content. Experts evaluate sources by checking their reputation elsewhere first, not by reading their claims in isolation.

faq.question: Why is corroboration from independent sources so important?
faq.answer: A single source can be biased, mistaken, or fabricated. When multiple independent sources reach the same conclusion through different methods, the probability of error drops dramatically. Independence is what gives corroboration its power.
